\chapter{Children and Everybody --- Boy, Girl, Lad, Lass, People}
\label{ch:ninos-y-gente}
\hlchaptermodality{308}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can talk about children and about people in general in Spanish, and I can tell a real cousin word from a false friend.}

Complete ES-C308-gente: name children in both genders and move from one child to people in general.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el niño]{el niño --- the word with no ancestors}

\label{lesson:ES-C308-nino}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el niño} --- \textquotedblleft{}the boy,\textquotedblright{} or a child of either sex when you do not need to say which.

Every word so far in this chapter has had a Latin pedigree. This one has none. \emph{Niño} comes from \textbf{ninno}, which is nursery babble --- the noise adults make at small children, frozen into a word.

That is not a failure of the word. English does exactly the same thing: \emph{baby} and \emph{babe} are \emph{bab-} babbling sounds, \emph{papa} and \emph{mama} are the two easiest noises a mouth can make. Languages build their most intimate words out of the sounds infants produce, which is why those words rarely resemble their neighbours.

English does know this one, though, and untranslated. \textbf{El Niño} --- the Pacific warming named by Peruvian fishermen because it arrives near Christmas --- is \textquotedblleft{}the boy,\textquotedblright{} meaning the Christ child. You have been saying \emph{niño} on weather forecasts your whole life.

The \textbf{ñ} is its own letter, not an n with decoration.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word you already knew from the weather report.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el niño}
  \item \emph{el niño y el hijo}
  \item \emph{el nombre del niño, por favor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does \emph{niño} come from Latin? (No --- nursery babble.) What is \emph{El Niño} literally? (The boy --- the Christ child.) Which English words are built the same way? (\emph{Baby}, \emph{mama}, \emph{papa}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la niña]{la niña --- the little figure in the eye}

\label{lesson:ES-C308-nina}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la niña} --- \textquotedblleft{}the girl.\textquotedblright{}

The ending switch, on a word with no Latin behind it. \textbf{La Niña} is the cold counterpart to \emph{El Niño}, named afterwards to match.

Now the good one. In Spanish, \textbf{la niña del ojo} is the \emph{pupil} of the eye --- \textquotedblleft{}the little girl of the eye.\textquotedblright{} Lean close to somebody's eye and you see a tiny figure of yourself reflected in the dark centre. Spanish named the pupil after that little person.

English named it the same way and hid the fact behind Latin. \emph{Pupil} is Latin \textbf{pupilla}, \textquotedblleft{}little doll\textquotedblright{} --- the same tiny reflected figure, the same observation, made independently. And that is why \emph{pupil} also means a schoolchild: \emph{pupilla} was a small girl first.

Two languages looked into an eye, saw a child, and both named it that.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Twelve words, and proof that two languages can invent the same metaphor.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la niña}
  \item \emph{el niño y la niña}
  \item \emph{la niña y la prima}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{la niña del ojo}? (The pupil.) Why? (The tiny figure reflected in it.) What is English \emph{pupil} in Latin? (\emph{Pupilla}, little doll --- the same idea.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el chico]{el chico --- small first, boy second}

\label{lesson:ES-C308-chico}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el chico} --- \textquotedblleft{}the boy,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the lad.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{ciccum} was the thin membrane inside a pomegranate --- the Roman byword for something worth nothing at all, the way English says \emph{not worth a fig}. From \textquotedblleft{}a trifle\textquotedblright{} it slid to \textquotedblleft{}tiny,\textquotedblright{} and from \textquotedblleft{}tiny\textquotedblright{} to \textquotedblleft{}a small person.\textquotedblright{}

This word has no English descendant, and that absence is worth a moment: not every Spanish word has a cousin waiting in English. The method works because so many do, not because all of them must.

Two things to keep straight. First, \emph{chico} still means \emph{small} before it means \emph{boy}, and you will meet it as an adjective constantly. Second, English \emph{chick} for a young bird looks like a match and is not --- that is a Germanic word, and the resemblance is an accident. A look-alike with no shared ancestor is called a false friend, and this is your first one.

Meanwhile American English has borrowed the feminine, \emph{chica}, outright.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word that arrived by meaning small --- and your first false friend.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el chico}
  \item \emph{el chico y el niño}
  \item \emph{el chico, por favor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{ciccum}? (The papery skin in a pomegranate --- a trifle.) What does \emph{chico} mean before it means boy? (Small.) Is English \emph{chick} related? (No --- a false friend.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la chica]{la chica --- the loan running backwards}

\label{lesson:ES-C308-chica}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la chica} --- \textquotedblleft{}the girl.\textquotedblright{}

Same root, same switch. What is different is the direction of travel.

Nearly every word so far has come \emph{to} Spanish and \emph{to} English out of Latin, or has been borrowed by English from somewhere older. \emph{Chica} went the other way. American English took it directly from Spanish, in living memory, without translating it --- and it is now printed in English dictionaries.

That happens far more than the Latin story suggests. English also took \emph{plaza}, \emph{patio}, \emph{cargo}, \emph{canyon} and \emph{ranch} straight from Spanish. When you learn Spanish you are not only meeting new words; you are meeting the source of words you already own.

The \textbf{ch} is a single letter's worth of sound, exactly as in English \emph{chair}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Fourteen words --- and one that English got from Spanish, not the reverse.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la chica}
  \item \emph{el chico y la chica}
  \item \emph{la chica y la niña}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which way did \emph{chica} travel? (Spanish into English.) Name another word English took from Spanish. (\emph{Plaza}, \emph{patio}, \emph{canyon}, \emph{ranch}.) How is \emph{ch} pronounced? (As in \emph{chair}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la gente]{la gente --- everybody, from one clan}

\label{lesson:ES-C308-gente}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la gente} --- \textquotedblleft{}people.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{gens} was a clan: everyone descended from a single ancestor. It is the word Rome used to sort its families, and it has been extremely busy in English.

\emph{Gentle} meant \textquotedblleft{}of good family\textquotedblright{} long before it meant \textquotedblleft{}soft\textquotedblright{} --- a \emph{gentleman} was a man with a \emph{gens} worth naming, and the softness is a later assumption about how such men behaved. \emph{Genteel} is the same word borrowed a second time, through French. A \emph{Gentile} is somebody of the other nations, the other clans. And \emph{general} is what applies to the whole kind rather than one case.

Two things about using it. The \textbf{g} before an \textbf{e} is not the g of \emph{gato} --- it is the throat sound, the same as the j in \emph{jota}. And \emph{la gente} is grammatically singular even though it means many people, the way English treats \emph{the public}.

So the word for everybody started as the word for one family.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Fifteen words, and a root that has been hiding in English manners all along.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la gente}
  \item \emph{la gente y la familia}
  \item \emph{mucha gente, señora}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was a \emph{gens}? (A clan from one ancestor.) What did \emph{gentle} originally mean? (Of good family.) How is the g in \emph{gente} pronounced? (As a jota, not as in \emph{gato}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
